Title: Exogenous social norms shift fisheries compliance under inadequate enforcement: Insights from a novel experiment
Authors: Stuart T. Jones, Joshua Cinner, Vera te Velde, Chris Wilcox, Brock Bergseth

Title: Sustainable and inclusive wellbeing governance: Reinventing democracy after the crisis
Authors: Robert Costanza, Roberto De Vogli, Sandrine Dixson-Decléve, Lorenzo Fioramonti, Enrico Giovannini, Ida Kubiszewski, Hunter Lovins, Jacqueline McGlade, Lars Fogh Mortensen, Kate E. Pickett, Kristín Vala Ragnarsdóttir, Stewart Wallis, Richard Wilkinson
Abstract: Despite decades of advances in sustainability science, global progress on climate change, biodiversity loss, inequality, and human wellbeing remains dangerously inadequate. While these failures are often attributed to insufficient political will or contested knowledge, we argue that a more fundamental constraint lies in how collective decisions are made. Contemporary governance systems are increasingly shaped by concentrated economic and political power, undermining their capacity to act in the collective interest and to pursue long-term sustainability goals. At the same time, there is growing evidence that citizens broadly support transformative policies aimed at sustainable and inclusive wellbeing. We argue that governance design itself has become a critical leverage point for sustainability transitions. For example, deliberative democracy offers an alternative by representing shared societal values and goals through randomly selected citizens' assemblies. Such assemblies operate independently of partisan and special-interest control and have demonstrated success at several scales. Advances in communication technology now make their broad application increasingly feasible. In parallel, new decision-making methods, such as sociocracy, emphasise consent over majority rule and provide tools to reduce polarization and foster inclusive agreements within deliberative processes. Viewed historically, today's governance challenges resemble recurrent crises and may offer a critical opening to adopt more sustainable and inclusive forms of governance, grounded in deliberation, consent, and collective wellbeing.

Title: Indiscriminate barriers: The trade effects of due diligence policies in global timber markets
Authors: Valentin Mathieu, Clément Nedoncelle

Title: Hydropower dams, deforestation, and land use change: Evidence from Brazil
Authors: Chiara Falco, Valentina Raimondi
Abstract: In Brazil, hydropower generates more than 60% of the national electricity supply, placing the country among the most hydropower-dependent economies worldwide. This study analyses the causal impact of dam construction on forest loss in Brazil using a new municipality-level panel dataset covering 379 dams, combined with high-resolution satellite data on forest coverage, among other variables. Applying modern staggered differenceindifferences estimators and a dynamic event study, we find that dams reduce forest cover by almost 9% percent in the municipality. No anticipatory effects are detected, but postconstruction losses increase steadily over time. Mechanism show that forest loss occurs mainly through cropland expansion, with smaller increases in pasture and higher agricultural value added. Effects are concentrated in the North and NorthEast regions, amplified in municipalities with high public land shares and unequal land distribution, consistent with persistent institutional legacies. Our results highlight that while hydropower enhances energy security, it entails substantial environmental costs requiring stronger land governance.

Title: Toward low-carbon diets: Exploring the role of climate perceptions and household mitigation practices in reducing meat consumption
Authors: Lan Tran, Ye Su

Title: Tax-financed green policies and income inequality in an agent-based model
Authors: Lucca Gustafson Rodrigues, Gilberto Tadeu Lima, Pedro Romero Marques
Abstract: The interdependent dynamics among economic growth, income inequality, and greenhouse gas emissions have attracted attention in both academic and policy discussions on decarbonization strategies. Notwithstanding this expanding body of work, theoretical and empirical contributions underscore the difficulty of simultaneously achieving favorable outcomes across these three dimensions, suggesting the existence of a structural trilemma involving growth, income distribution, and environmental degradation. This paper develops an agent-based model (ABM) to explore these trade-offs and focuses on the impacts of different tax-financed green policies. Financing and environmental policy instruments produce complex effects on key macroeconomic variables, raising questions about whether—and under what conditions—the trilemma holds. The simulations examine scenarios in which either a carbon tax or a wealth tax finance the following green policies: (i) green price subsidy, (ii) public non-patented green R&D, (iii) subsidy for private green R&D, and (iv) green public procurement. While the carbon tax is both a financing and an environmental policy instrument, the wealth tax is primarily a mechanism of income redistribution. Findings suggest that the policy mix is a key determinant of whether the trilemma might occur. On the one hand, carbon taxation is more effective in reducing emissions but at higher social and macroeconomic costs. On the other hand, despite promoting redistribution, wealth taxation must count on specific complementary policies—such as public-led green innovation—to foster a low-carbon economy.

Title: Decoupling transition patterns in the global economy: A multi-regional structural decomposition analysis
Authors: Waka Nishifuji, Shigemi Kagawa

Title: Biodiversity benefits of the climate adaptation policy: Evidence from millions birdwatching records in China

Title: From scarcity to strategy: Designing hay markets to mitigate feed shortages and income shocks
Authors: Julia Kunkel, Jonathan Haag, Robert Finger, Sergei Schaub, Jürgen Groeneveld, Christian Klassert, Birgit Müller
Abstract: Grassland-based forages — such as grass, silage, and hay — are a key feed source for dairy cows. In the transition to more sustainable dairy systems, grassland-based production is increasingly valued for its contributions to biodiversity and regional resilience. However, droughts reduce grassland yields and raise feed prices, challenging farmers to secure feed and stable incomes. Existing coping strategies, such as early slaughter or livestock sales, can have long-term consequences beyond the drought event. In this study, we propose hay markets as a short-term buffer for drought-induced feed shortages and income shocks. We compare potential trading networks differing in trading radius and trading partners in terms of effectiveness, efficiency and possible side effects using a stylised network model. For farm units aggregated at the German county level, we simulate cost-minimal trading schedules and derive remaining feed shortages and income shocks. Results show that forage trading can reduce shocks by around two-third during nationwide droughts and fully mitigate localised shocks. Effective mitigation requires either a broad trading radius or sufficient trading partners. However, poorly connected nationwide networks can lead to inefficient transport, while segmentation at state level may lock in shortages and reduce both effectiveness and efficiency. We also observe unintended side effects: trading may shift income shocks to unaffected farm units and increase overall transport distances. Overall, we show that hay markets could enhance dairy farmers’ drought resistance, but must be designed carefully. Policy makers, farmer associations, and agricultural chambers can support this by providing a well-designed market infrastructure.

Title: Between resistance and readiness: Segment-specific reactions to consumption reduction
Authors: Charlotte Baar, Saskia Flachs, Petra Riefler, Oliver B. Büttner
Abstract: Limiting global warming to 1.5 °C requires not only technological innovation but also substantial reductions in individual consumption, particularly in high-income societies. Yet, sufficiency lifestyles evoke divergent expectations among individuals including gains and losses that act as enablers or barriers to adopting such lifestyles. Effective communication efforts aiming at promoting lifestyle uptake should be informed about existing consumer stances on this idea. Using a sample of Austrian consumers and latent class analysis, we identify five consumer segments that differ in their engagement with sufficiency-oriented lifestyles, from highly engaged to highly disengaged. These segments vary systematically in the benefits versus costs they anticipate from changing their lifestyles to support environmental goals. Anticipated satisfaction or frustration of autonomy, competence, and relatedness needs is linked to the likelihood of belonging to specific segments. The findings reveal distinct psychological profiles associated with individuals' position on sufficiency as a demand-side mitigation strategy and emphasize the importance of audience-tailored communication.

Title: Technology as the material ‘how’ of socio-ecological (re)production: Reflections on Wassily Leontief's ‘technological structure of the economy’
Authors: Miriam Boyer, Carlos López-Morales, Mathis Favre
Abstract: Wassily Leontief is widely known for his development of an applied approach in economics known as input-output (IO). In this paper, we turn to Leontief's analysis to reconstruct a concept of technology based on his work. The concept rests upon an analysis of Leontief's epistemological-methodological assumptions and the premises of his input-output model regarding interdependence. We argue that Leontief's concept of technology highlights the physical process of technology in two senses: As concrete flows of material stuff used in economic production in the sense of a particular ‘recipe’; but also as emergent systemic effects of that particular ‘recipe’ throughout an economy, or indeed throughout a socio-ecological system. This contrasts with other approaches in the social sciences that understand the materiality of technology largely in terms of objects, artifacts, and infrastructure. We argue that future research could benefit from incorporating Leontief's approach with work elsewhere in the social sciences. On the one hand, IO depictions of quantitative and systemic effects could be complemented by aspects that are not explicit in Leontief's framework, including specific social relations such as power, and the role of certain actors or conflicts. On the other, Leontief's emphasis on physical material aspects and their systemic effects can also link nicely with ecological research, even beyond the now common environmental extensions of the IO model. We argue that such work could yield interesting synergies in the future, not least in the field of ecological economics.

Title: Corrigendum to ‘The distributional impact of climate policy stringency in the European Union, Ecological Economics 249 (2026) [109118]’

Title: Food system actors perspectives on Swedish agricultural preparedness -a Q-methodology study

Title: Welfare implications of no net loss policies with heterogeneous cultural ecosystem services
Authors: Cathrine Hagem
Abstract: No net loss (NNL) targets for nature are increasingly implemented at both national and subnational levels. While these policies are typically framed in terms of area or biophysical equivalence, they may overlook heterogeneity in the cultural ecosystem service (CES) values associated with undeveloped land. This paper develops a parsimonious economic model to analyze the welfare implications of alternative NNL policy designs when CES values differ across municipalities. We distinguish between local CES values, such as recreational and amenity benefits accruing to nearby populations, and a national CES value associated with the existence of undeveloped nature. We compare unilateral and cooperative municipal policies and examine the performance of taxes and subsidies versus offset markets under area-based and CES value-based NNL targets. We show that area-based NNL policies are generally welfare suboptimal in the presence of heterogeneous local CES values, even when implemented cost-effectively through offset markets. By contrast, NNL targets defined in CES value terms can achieve constrained welfare optima using appropriately designed fiscal instruments or ambient permit markets. Although inter-municipal cooperation reduces aggregate costs, distributional effects may prevent mutually beneficial outcomes without side payments. Numerical illustrations based on Norwegian data support the analytical results and highlight implications for subnational and national offset policy design.

Title: The appearance of democracy: How conditional payments reshape behavior among local leaders
Authors: Ivo Steimanis, Esther Blanco, Björn Vollan
Abstract: Monetary incentives are widely considered to promote democratic practices in local governance. We test this proposition by providing causal evidence from a lab-in-the-field experiment with local leaders (n=64) and their constituents (n=384) in rural Namibia's hybrid governance setting. Using a within-subject design, we introduced conditional payments to leaders for allowing constituents to vote on how to distribute a collective fund. A majority of leaders (64%) chose a democratic rule at baseline, and the payments did not significantly increase this share. The incentives caused a significant reduction in openly autocratic behavior, primarily through a shift toward a pseudo-democratic practice of appearing democratic while retaining unilateral decision-making. This reveals unintended consequences of the conditional incentives, fostering symbolic compliance where leaders appear democratic while retaining control. Exploratory analysis shows payments "crowd out" democracy among initially democratic leaders but "crowd in" pseudo-democracy among autocratic leaders, moderated by governing motivations. Our findings illustrate that conditional payments can fail to foster genuine democracy and caution against their prescriptive use in complex governance environments.

Title: Exploring the range of approaches for recruitment, facilitation, and qualitative methods in deliberative valuation: Evidence from 66 case studies
Authors: Chloe A. Jackson, Ryan S.D. Calder, Amir M. Gazar, Richard B. Howarth, Georgia Mavrommati

Title: How managed lake-level fluctuations affect waterfront property values: Evidence from a regulated lake system

Title: The UK’s middle-income dietary trap: High emissions, low nutrition
Authors: Yunhuan Gao, Pablo Piñero, Eduardo Aguilera, Martin Bruckner, Alberto Sanz Cobeña, He He, Christian Reynolds
Abstract: Dietary transitions driven by income disparity increasingly impose a dual burden on health and the climate. This study integrates the Nutrient Rich Food (NRF 9.3 ) index and Global Warming Potential (GWP) to evaluate the nutrition‑carbon trade-off in UK household food purchases in 2013. Our analysis reveals a “middle-income dietary trap”. Across Deciles 4–8, households increase their overall food purchases as income rises, but this expansion is dominated by carbon-intensive, nutrient-poor foods such as meats, dairy, sugars, and vegetable oils. As a consequence, calorie intake peaks while improvements in diet quality lag behind, and carbon emissions reach their highest levels among all income groups. This misalignment reflects a stage in which rising food quantity precedes nutritional gains, generating a dual burden of high‑carbon, low-nutrition diets. In contrast, high-income groups (Deciles 9–10) achieve modest improvements in both nutrition and carbon efficiency, associated with higher consumption of nutrient-dense, low-GWP foods such as vegetables, fruits, and seafood. These findings highlight a non-linear income-emission relationship, consistent with the Environmental Kuznets Curve hypothesis. Our decomposition analysis identifies two mechanisms shaping dietary carbon efficiency: a static opposition between expenditure and energy density, and a dynamic trade-off between nutrient density and the carbon intensity of nutrients. Policy interventions should adopt stage-specific strategies targeting middle-income households, where the dietary trap is driven by expenditure–structure imbalance, by steering substitution toward nutrient-dense, lower-carbon foods and accelerating structural dietary change.

Title: Climate change skepticism and farmers' responses to CO2e taxation
Authors: Kahsay Haile Zemo, Mette Termansen
Abstract: Agriculture is a major contributor to greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, yet it has largely been exempt from stricter environmental regulations, partly due to strong resistance from the sector. Across Europe, farmers' widespread opposition has often resulted in the weakening or rollback of ambitious environmental policies. In Denmark, the recent introduction of a CO2e (CO2-equivalent) tax on agricultural emissions, one of the first global attempts to directly target non-fossil fuel-based GHGs, has similarly prompted immediate organized farmer protests. This study examines whether and to what extent climate change skepticism (CCS) is associated with farmers' belief misalignment about the economic impact of the CO2e tax on agriculture, resistance to the tax, and adoption of climate mitigation measures, drawing on a survey of 981 Danish farmers. We find that climate skeptic farmers substantially overestimate the tax's negative impacts while discounting expert assessments. Climate neutral and skeptic farmers show greater opposition to the CO2e tax, with CCS strongly predicting resistance even after accounting for tax design, information, and farm characteristics. Higher CCS is also associated with lower adoption of climate mitigation measures, with participation in subsidized climate initiatives about 25% lower among skeptics compared with non-skeptics. These patterns are more pronounced among livestock producers than crop producers. Overall, the findings underscore the importance of climate-related beliefs in explaining variation in beliefs about policy impacts, policy acceptance, and behavioral responses.

Title: Scenario discovery for a just low-carbon transition
Authors: Nicola Campigotto, Marco Catola, André Cieplinski, Simone D’Alessandro, Tiziano Distefano, Pietro Guarnieri, Till Heydenreich

Title: Commoning mobilizations and institutional outcomes in Indian forests from colonial to postcolonial periods
Authors: Fiona Gladstone, Arun Agrawal

Title: Does the framing of environmental ethics matter for the effectiveness of environmental education? Evidence from field experiments in elementary schools
Authors: Akinori Kitsuki, Yoichiro Miki, Chiyoko Nagatani, Kazuhiro Nomoto, Toshio Sadakuni, Shigeharu Terui, Satoru Uchida, Asuka Yamamoto, Yuichiro Fujioka
Abstract: The importance of environmental ethics is broadly acknowledged in environmental education. Nevertheless, little is known about whether differences in teachers' framing of ethical perspectives can lead to significant differences in outcomes. This study addresses this gap through field experiments evaluating the short-term impact of classes on local conservation issues among students and their parents in 21 public elementary schools in Kushiro, Japan. Schools were randomly assigned to two groups: one began with a discussion of what blessings their local wetland brings to themselves (anthropocentric framing), and the other with what it brings to living creatures (ecocentric framing), with the remaining class content being the same. Results show that, although it was not observed that such differences in framing spilled over to parents, student interest improved only with anthropocentric framing. This finding suggests that anthropocentric framing can motivate students in the short run, but it should be noted that this does not imply that it is ethically superior. Rather, it suggests that educators who focus primarily on motivating student interest may unintentionally default to anthropocentric messaging, despite the value of ecocentrism. The results highlight the need to be intentional about how ethical perspectives are framed in practice, as well as the importance of a solid understanding of environmental ethics among educators.

Title: Socio-metabolic class conflicts in the Anthropocene
Authors: Ilona M. Otto, Toni Schuster
Abstract: The Anthropocene epoch is characterized by an excessive use of natural resources and energy that contributes to the environmental destruction of the planet. However, large inequalities exist among social groups that benefit to various degrees from the use of resources and energy, as well as among individuals suffering from the negative impacts of environmental destruction. In this paper, we systematically analyze these differences and discuss a social stratification theory based on these inequalities in terms of possessions, social status, ability to control and benefit from planetary material cycles and energy flows, or suffering due to the consequences of environmental degradation. Referring to consumption data, we propose six global socio-metabolic classes and show distinctive energy use patterns by these classes. More research is needed to determine differences in the use of natural resources needed to maintain the biosphere integrity, such as land, water, nitrogen, and phosphorus. To reduce existing inequalities, policies are needed that eliminate extreme poverty, improve education and healthcare access, promote decent living standards, and increase political representation of the underprivileged. In addition, policies that reduce extreme wealth accumulation and excessive consumption of energy and natural resources are needed to target the most privileged members of society.

Title: Human climate niche, habitability range, and economic growth
Authors: Jean-François Gajewski, Paul-Oliver Klein, Fatima Ezzahrae Tahri
Abstract: This study develops a contemporaneous measure of the human habitability of geographic areas, the Habitability Range that builds upon the work of Xu et al. (2020) on pretechnological human density in a temperature-precipitation climatic space. Using this measure with climatic data from 1901 to 2022, we document a 32.98% (−8.40 pp) global decline in human habitability over the past century. Using economic data from 181 countries (1950–2022), we find that a one standard deviation loss in habitability reduced GDP per capita by 4.24% at country level and by 2.46% at subnational level. While high Total Factor Productivity (TFP) reduces dependence on the climate niche, declines in habitability can lower TFP, thereby limiting adaptation capacities.

Title: Farmers’ preferences and attitudes in conversion to organic farming: A lab-in-the-field experiment
Authors: Tuan Nguyen-Anh, Phu Nguyen-Van, Nguyen To-The
Abstract: Despite rising organic food consumption, the transition to organic farming lags, particularly in developing countries, where only 2% of agricultural land was organic in 2022. To address this, we investigate how farmers’ elicited preferences (risk tolerance, ambiguity tolerance, and time preferences), social factors, and environmental attitudes shape their intention to convert land to organic farming. Using a lab-in-the-field experiment with 311 Vietnamese farmers, we apply a fractional regression model to analyze the intended percentage of land conversion. Results show that higher risk tolerance, higher ambiguity tolerance, future bias, pro-social preferences, perceived behavioral control, and social norms are positively associated with conversion intent, while environmental attitude lacks statistical significance. The revised robustness analysis shows that these patterns are stable when we account for outcome spikes and focal-point responses.

Title: Book Review
Authors: Ugo Bardi

Title: Willingness to pay for birdsong
Authors: Anthony Higney, Charlotte Gerling, Claire Buchan, Simon Butler, Liam Crowther, Melissa Marselle, Eleanor Ratcliffe, Konrad Uebel, Nick Hanley
Abstract: We present the first estimate of the causal effect of auditory sensation on willingness to pay and the first estimate of the marginal value of bird song, using constructed soundscapes. We compare willingness to pay values for increases in bird wildlife habitat quality and quantity between samples where respondents are played recordings of soundscapes compared to respondents who do not get to listen to these simulated soundscapes. Preferences for the costs of habitat restoration and willingness to pay for habitat quality enhancements were found to be significantly larger in the “with soundscapes” sample. Methodologically, this paper reports on the use of simulated soundscapes in choice experiments as a means of increasing the information respondents have before making their choices.

Title: From utopian impulse to urban engagement: The role of doughnut economics in shaping residents' participation in smart cities
Authors: Frédéric Basso, Norbert Lebrument, Corinne Rochette
Abstract: Smart cities are often framed through techno-utopian narratives, yet their capacity to support sustainable transitions depends on residents' engagement. This article examines how the transformative utopian impulse and support for the principles of Doughnut Economics shape residents' intention to participate in smart city projects. Drawing on a survey of 645 residents in five French cities (Paris, Lyon, Marseille, Lille and Toulouse), we estimate a model using partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) combined with Necessary Condition Analysis (NCA) to distinguish sufficient from necessary causal relations. PLS-SEM results show that the transformative utopian impulse significantly influences participatory intention, both directly and indirectly through support for Doughnut Economics principles. NCA complements these findings by revealing that both constructs operate as necessary conditions for high levels of participatory intention, with support for Doughnut Economics emerging as the most critical precondition for high levels of participatory intention: while it contributes relatively little as a direct average driver of participation, its absence effectively prevents residents from reaching the highest levels of engagement. This “axiological” threshold effect indicates that commitment to post-growth principles shifts from secondary to indispensable as participation intensifies. The study advances urban governance research by moving beyond the opposition between technology-centric smart city agendas and post-growth urbanism: Doughnut Economics functions as an intermediary normative framework translating utopian aspirations into more concrete forms of urban engagement. For practitioners, the results highlight that participatory mechanisms must be coupled with coherent value frameworks if smart city programmes are to mobilise residents for transformative and sustainability-oriented projects.

Title: How justice shapes local support for grassland conservation program: A mixed-methods research
Authors: Ruxin Zhang, Zhuohui Ye

Title: From domestic collapse to global dispersion: Post-Fukushima carbon redistribution
Authors: Tong Su

Title: Limited and unintended effects of climate, health, and animal welfare labels
Authors: Amelie Griesoph, Thomas Schreiner, Christine Merk, Stefan Hoffmann, Katrin Rehdanz, Ulrich Schmidt

Title: Beyond resilience: Domestic and cross-border economic impacts and co-benefits of regional climate change adaptation
Authors: Dimitrios Stamopoulos, Petros Dimas, Ioannis Sebos, Dionysis Assimacopoulos

Title: The costs of social and environmental degradation in affluent economies
Authors: Giulia Slater, Francesco Sarracino
Abstract: I ndividuals’ attempts to defend from the deterioration of common goods, such as natural and social capital, stimulate defensive growth, that is new economic activity driven by private solutions to collective problems. In this paper, we provide an estimate of the value of defensive expenditures - the individual consumption needed to protect subjective well-being against collective problems - using a compensating differentials approach; that is we estimate the monetary valuation of social and environmental disruption for which no market price exists. To do so, we conduct a regression analysis of life satisfaction on aggregate consumption levels and various social and environmental externalities (which we refer to as "bads"). Our estimates indicate that the consumption needed to defend against collective problems is worth nearly a quarter of actual individual consumption. In terms of national income, this is equivalent to nearly half Gross Domestic Product per capita in affluent economies. Defensive consumption stimulates economic growth, however, in so far as the equivalent of nearly half of growth is defensive, its expansion does not reflect true progress.

Title: Wealth taxes for an eco-social transition: How different tax designs align with post-growth goals
Authors: Thomas Webb, Arthur Apostel, Milena Büchs, Richard Bärnthaler
Abstract: Wealth taxes are frequently proposed within the post-growth policy literature, but evaluations of their alignment with post-growth goals, and empirical estimates of their potential effects, are lacking. We contribute to this literature by examining the extent to which different wealth tax designs can contribute to four goals of a post-growth transition: redistributing wealth; eradicating extreme wealth; curbing rent-seeking; and reducing CO 2 emissions. The analysis is based on microsimulation modelling, using household-level data from 18 countries of the 2017 EU Household Finance and Consumption Survey. It shows that broad-based net wealth taxes with lower thresholds and higher rates are most effective for maximising revenue, reducing top 10% wealth shares, limiting extreme wealth, and lowering inequality-related CO₂ emissions; more targeted net wealth taxes with higher thresholds and rates maximise progressivity and reduce top 1% wealth concentration; while taxes on financial and investment property wealth tend to be most effective at curbing rent extraction (all else equal). However, we also identify trade-offs and conflicts between different tax designs and goals. As a result, a broader package of policies will be necessary to navigate these conflicts and mitigate the limitations inherent in any single wealth tax design.

Title: Water justice: Empirical analysis of U.S. patterns and regional heterogeneity
Authors: Zoey Reed-Spitzer, Bonnie G. Colby
Abstract: Water quality, water access and competition among competing water uses are a concern around the globe. In many areas of the U.S., water availability is constrained by pollution and lack of water delivery and treatment infrastructure. These constraints have disproportionate effects on low-income areas and communities of color. In this article, we analyze differential exposure among racial and ethnic groups to specific environmental burdens linked to how water is used and managed. We examine differential exposure by analyzing data from the U.S Council on Environmental Quality, combined with U.S. census data for 73,225 census tracts covering the entire U.S. We find that Hispanic and Black populations are disproportionately exposed to three of the environmental burdens examined in this study: dust pollution, leaky underground storage tanks and lack of green space. Black and American Indian populations are more likely to be in census tracts with higher proportions of inadequate household water access. We also document substantial regional heterogeneity in these patterns, with disparities among groups varying significantly in magnitude across U.S. regions. Identifying systemic patterns of differential exposure is a first step in motivating and shaping policy measures to mitigate disproportional adverse effects on vulnerable populations.

Title: Modeling for post-growth: Backcasting radical futures
Authors: Thibaut Feix, Nadia Maïzi
Abstract: Economic models are more than technical instruments: they are lenses that shape our understanding of reality and our ability to address contemporary challenges. They embed ethical commitments, political assumptions, and institutional framings that influence their outputs. We illustrate how normative and positive modeling approaches anchor their projections in existing economic structures through what we call structural induction. This effect is further reinforced by the way models frame scenarios. In the context of post-growth, these framing effects limit the capacity to explore radical narratives. To overcome these limitations, we advocate a backcasting approach, beginning with detailed qualitative narratives of proposed futures and using models iteratively to check their consistency and explore them quantitatively. In this way, models are used as exploratory tools, probing uncertain terrain rather than producing projections. This approach calls for the development of comprehensive and shared post-growth narratives. We then propose a conceptual classification of models, based on Daly's ends-means spectrum, to cover the range of post-growth concerns: need-oriented modeling, social and physical provisioning systems modeling, and biophysical modeling. Reviewing recent modeling exercises through this lens, we observe that biophysical modeling is gaining increasing attention, while need-oriented modeling remains underexplored despite its central importance for representing post-growth futures. Finally, we discuss the need for the modeling community to adopt a critical stance toward models and to explicitly define criteria for their validity.

Title: Eating nature: Revealing the ecological cost of food trade through a global biodiversity-risk footprint
Authors: Stella Lauro, Silvana Dalmazzone, Giorgio Vacchiano, Marco M. Bagliani
Abstract: International trade in food commodities is a major driver of global biodiversity loss through the conversion of forests to agriculture. Yet existing deforestation metrics often fail to capture the full ecological consequences. We introduce a Biodiversity Risk indicator that weights deforested hectares by species vulnerability and endemism, offering a more nuanced assessment of biodiversity impacts from agricultural expansion into forests. Linking spatially explicit deforestation data with food trade flows, we uncover strong mismatches between countries’ Deforestation Footprint and Biodiversity Risk. Indonesia, despite lower deforestation volumes than Brazil, emerges as the most impacted country due to high species vulnerability and specific crop conversion patterns. Commodity-level analysis distinguishes locally consumed crops (e.g., meat, cassava, rice) from globally traded biodiversity-intensive commodities (e.g., palm oil, soy, natural rubber), offering new insights for targeted interventions. Our findings underscore the need to integrate biodiversity metrics into supply-chain governance and deforestation policies to promote more ecologically responsible trade.

Title: The false certainties of climate policy: Rethinking risk and cooperation in an uncertain future
Authors: John-Oliver Engler, Florian Ulrich Jehn, Astrid Kause, Henrik von Wehrden, Jana Zscheischler, Johann Majer

Title: Energy, surplus and the economic process
Authors: Giorgos Kallis, Claudio Cattaneo, Angelos Varvarousis, Marula Tsagkari, Marta Conde, Giacomo D'Alisa, Ksenija Hanaček, Borja Nogué-Algueró, Filka Sekulova, Aljoša Slameršak
Abstract: This paper analyses the economic process through the concept of surplus, combining insights from ecological economics, Marxist political economy and anthropology. Humans, we argue, appropriate surplus energy with their labor from nature and apply it to transform matter into goods and services, with entropy increasing along the way. How societies distribute and expend their surpluses gives them some of their signature features. In hierarchical societies, the ruling classes control a great share of the surplus and expend it in ways that reproduce their power. Economic growth, a distinctive feature of capitalist civilization, is the result of the ruling capitalist class investing surplus in the means of production in order to make more surplus. Surplus is extracted both via technological innovation that increases productivity and by social domination that reduces the share of surplus that goes back to workers or nature. Growth, however, is not only a material process but also a hegemonic story told by the capitalist class to dress its private interest as general interest, legitimating control over the destiny of surplus. Our framework proposes a political, ecological-economic theory of growth, provides a foundation for analyzing degrowth, and sheds new light on longstanding debates between ecological economists and Marxists.

Title: Pro-social versus pro-self motivations for green roof adoption: Evidence from a discrete choice experiment
Authors: Georges Farina, Peter J. Robinson, W.J. Wouter Botzen, Pieter Van Beukering
Abstract: Green roofs are a promising Nature-Based Solution (NBS) for urban climate adaptation, yet their adoption remains limited due to multiple factors, including mixed incentives between private and public benefits. This study investigates the impact of information nudges on public preferences and willingness-to-pay (WTP) for green roof co-benefits in the Netherlands. Using a split-sample ( n = 2173) Discrete Choice Experiment (DCE), we examine how highlighting private (e.g., indoor cooling, roof lifespan) versus public (e.g., biodiversity, flood risk reduction) benefits influences WTP. The results show that respondents value green roof benefits overall highly. Information nudges significantly affect WTP for specific attributes. In particular, the Pro-self treatment, that communicates the private benefits of green roofs, increases WTP for indoor cooling and flood risk reduction, while the Pro-social treatment, communicating the public benefits, positively influences preferences for biodiversity improvements. Our findings suggest that even when information emphasizes private benefits, it can simultaneously enhance WTP for collective outcomes, likely due to perceived spillover effects. The preferences also display a high level of heterogeneity, indicating diverse valuation patterns within the population. The study further highlights that focusing individuals on their private gains is an effective strategy to increase their support for green roofs. This result is particularly salient for households that rank low on the altruism scale. Additionally, the high demand for biodiversity suggests that cost-benefit analyses should account for non-use values when evaluating green roof policies.

Title: Land-use optimization to support cost-effective landscape transformation policies for wildfire mitigation
Authors: Rui Serôdio Simões, Paulo Flores Ribeiro, Marta Mesquita, Isabel Martins, João Morais Mourato, José Lima Santos

Title: The impact of climate on Indian households' living costs
Authors: Yuhang Qu, David J. Maddison, Robert J.R. Elliott, Eric Strobl
Abstract: • We calculate climate equivalence scales for Indian households. • Climate makes an appreciable difference to households' living costs. • Indian households prefer a climate not characterised by extremes. • High humidity is particularly costly to Indian households.

Title: Humanity does not play DICE: A sensitivity analysis of technical progress
Authors: Antoine Ronsain, Alexandre Gondran, Estelle Malavolti
Abstract: The DICE model claims that technological progress can prevent global warming at low cost. However, its conclusions are predicated on highly optimistic and contested assumptions regarding the costs and effectiveness of backstop technologies, as well as the magnitude of climate damages. This study assesses the robustness of the DICE model’s recommendations by exploring their sensitivity to these core assumptions. We investigate scenarios where assumptions prove to be more pessimistic than DICE standard baseline. We employ a large-scale scenario-based analysis to account for the possible range of the climate damage function and the level of efficiency of future backstop technologies, as well as their financial costs. Our results demonstrate that relying on technology alone is a very risky bet; under a wide spectrum of plausible, less optimistic assumptions, 84 % of scenarios lead to a climate-induced economic collapse. To address this fragility, we introduce a social lever into the model: economic sufficiency, defined as the policy option to produce less than the maximum production capacity. The inclusion of this lever dramatically alters the outcomes if the social-planner is enough forward looking. Our study concludes that relying on purely technological solutions is a hazardous strategy under uncertainty and that a dual strategy, combining both technological and social levers, is required to reduce the risk of climate collapse.

Title: Limits to growth revisited: System dynamics simulations of global economic developments and distributional implications in the 21st century
Authors: Arthur Lauer, Luis Llases
Abstract: We use a system dynamics environment-economy model to explore how multiple limits to growth may affect global economic output and consumption across different social classes until 2100. Based on a five-dimensional scenario space, we simulate global economic development in 120 scenarios that differ in labor productivity growth, per-capita consumption growth, fossil resource availability, climate change severity, and climate system sensitivity. In 92% of the simulations, output peaks and then declines persistently. Excluding scenarios without climate impacts, output in 2100 is 15–70% lower than in 2019. Scenarios with low labor productivity and consumption growth experience earlier peaks at lower levels and moderate output declines. In contrast, scenarios with high labor productivity and consumption growth show faster and longer periods of growth but eventually face economic collapse. While resource depletion and climate damages act as stressors, most simulations indicate that growth ultimately halts and reverses due to a shortage of labor hours. During the phase of unintentional economic degrowth, economic convergence and redistribution reduce consumption in high-income countries to values 3–4 times lower than initial consumption levels, while middle- and low-income countries return to consumption levels similar to those at the start of the simulations. Poverty reduction in poorer regions ends as global output peaks, while environmental destabilization caused by economic growth threatens development opportunities beyond the 21st century.

Title: Ecological macroeconomics meets community-led modelling: localising ecological macroeconomics through participatory system dynamics
Authors: Katrina Szetey, Enayat A. Moallemi, Brett A. Bryan
Abstract: Understanding how local economies and wellbeing evolve under ecological constraints is central to ecological macroeconomic modelling, but local-scale applications remain limited. We co-produced a participatory system dynamics model with a small rural community in south-eastern Australia to explore alternative local futures. Six scenarios (the local socioeconomic pathways) were developed collaboratively, integrating community priorities and values into both qualitative narratives and quantitative model parameters. Our approach combined participatory scenario development, community-led modelling, and quantitative pathway analysis, including sensitivity and uncertainty assessments. This enabled a systematic exploration of alternative futures and the trade-offs between social, environmental, and economic dimensions. The results revealed that scenarios prioritising economic growth exhibited greater uncertainty, while those emphasising social and environmental dimensions, particularly a low-growth pathway, delivered more robust and desirable sustainability outcomes for the community. The community-led modelling process enhanced the legitimacy, transparency, and relevance of the results, supporting informed decision-making and enabling stakeholders to navigate complex trade-offs and uncertainties. This research demonstrates the value of integrating participatory and quantitative approaches for place-based planning, and highlights how community-scale modelling can extend ecological macroeconomic thinking by making distributional outcomes, constraints, and robustness visible in local decisions.

Title: Effective establishment of circularity is key to achieving net zero

Title: Income inequality and the trade-off between socio-economic and ecological goals
Authors: Svenja Flechtner, Martin Middelanis
Abstract: No country currently achieves basic social needs without exceeding ecological limits, yet the environmental cost of attaining given living standards differs substantially across countries. This paper examines whether income inequality moderates this trade-off. Unlike much of the literature, which emphasizes within-country dynamics, we focus on cross-country variation. Employing a cross-sectional time-series panel of 124 countries from 1992–2015, we estimate models with Mundlak decompositions that isolate between-country differences. Our results show contrasting patterns: in low- and high-income countries, greater income equality is linked with lower environmental costs at a given standard of living. In contrast, in middle-income countries, greater inequality is associated with lower ecological damage. We interpret these differences through variation in the marginal propensity to consume and to emit, suggesting that distributive structures shape how societies navigate the trade-off between living standards and environmental sustainability.

Title: Municipal solid waste generation in Norway: A panel analysis investigating the waste Kuznets curve
Authors: Kim Rainer Mattson, Julia Sborz, Elisa Henning, Juudit Ottelin
Abstract: Municipal Solid Waste (MSW) generation is a considerable issue in terms of environmental pollution and is inextricably linked to household consumption. To identify potential decoupling of economic activity and waste, studies have tested the Waste Kuznets Curve (WKC) hypothesis, investigating factors that increase or decrease the MSW per capita generation across and within countries. We analyze a panel data set of 344 municipalities in Norway between 2006 and 2023, identifying variables that influence MSW generation both at the general and the individual municipality level. Three panel regression models are estimated, these being Fixed Effect, pooled Ordinary Least Squares, and system Generalized Method of Moments. We find evidence of relative decoupling between income and MSW/capita, however, at income levels and a timeframe that arguably makes actual decoupling unlikely under current modes of consumption. We find that vacation home practice is a significant driver of higher MSW generation, and that periods of interest rate hikes reduce MSW generation, showing the importance of addressing specific socio-cultural contexts. We also observed no significant effect of national policy implementation instruments included in our study design over the investigated period. Although our model approach and selection are robust, accounting for endogeneity and unobserved heterogeneity of the panel data, systematic non-reporting of MSW occurring outside municipal households at the regional level provides a challenge, obscuring the possible qualitative difference between urban and rural environments. This is a significant issue for much of the WKC literature and represents a clear research gap for future studies.

Title: Democratically planned degrowth: Modeling for rapid climate crisis mitigation

Title: A holistic assessment of farmers' intention to adopt agroecological practices – The case of Swiss grassland
Authors: Andreia Arbenz, Gabriele Mack, Jeanine Ammann, Niklas Möhring
Abstract: Agroecology provides a holistic approach to sustainable agriculture. Although the concept is gaining increasing interest, there is a lack of knowledge regarding farmers' intentions to adopt agroecological practices, and existing studies do not account for its holistic approach. We analyze farmers' intentions to adopt agroecological practices across four key elements of agroecology: diversity, synergy, efficiency, and recycling. We assess a wide range of potential drivers, including farm and farmer characteristics, natural conditions, expected opportunity costs, and behavioral factors. Our focus is on grassland farming in the Swiss mountain region, a production system with high agroecological potential. We combine survey data collected between April and May 2024 from 495 farmers, with agricultural census data and weather data. Our analysis shows that farmers' intentions to adopt agroecology are highest for practices related to recycling, followed by practices that increase synergies, farm diversity, and efficiency. Further, we find that social norms (i.e., injunctive norms, descriptive norms, and signaling motives) are key drivers for scaling up agroecology across all elements. Economic factors primarily relate to the adoption of elements of agroecology especially where higher investments (i.e., solar panels and biogas) are required. The results suggest that measures focusing on farmers' social norms, such as nudges or information campaigns, could support scaling up agroecology. Further, our results highlight the multifaceted nature of agroecology, particularly its interconnected elements and the importance of behavioral factors for adoption intentions. We conclude that a one-size-fits-all approach to the different elements of agroecology is unlikely to be efficient in scaling up agroecology.

Title: What drives the spatiotemporal evolution of land use conflicts? Evidence of threshold effects from 19 Chinese urban agglomerations

Title: Unpacking households' environmental footprint: Comparing price and quantity effects in Flemish food consumption
Authors: Michiel Pauwels, Kaat Verbist, Maarten Christis, An Vercalsteren, Luc Alaerts, Karel Van Acker
Abstract: Household food consumption is a major driver of environmental impacts, yet existing assessments often overlook how household characteristics shape these impacts. Most studies rely on expenditure-based approaches that assume constant elasticities between spending and environmental pressure. This study reassesses the role of income and other household characteristics by contrasting expenditure-based and functional-unit approaches to measuring food consumption. We combine data from the 2022 Belgian Household Budget Survey with a detailed life cycle assessment database to estimate environmental impacts for Flemish households. We use log–log OLS regressions to evaluate how household characteristics influence food demand measured in quantities and expenditures, as well as the associated environmental footprints. Dominance analysis is applied to assess relative contribution of each characteristic to explained variance. The results challenge the assumption that higher income proportionally increases food-related environmental impacts. Across product groups, income elasticities are higher for expenditures than for quantities. The global warming footprint ranges from 3.0 to 3.6 tons CO₂-equivalent across income groups, a narrower spread than in previous studies. Household size and composition are the main drivers of variation, with larger households exhibiting lower per-capita impacts, consistent with economies of scale. Age is also significant, as older households tend toward consumption patterns linked to higher-impact food categories. By contrast, households in smaller dwellings and more urbanized areas tend to have lower impacts. These findings highlight the importance of methodological choices in environmental impact assessment and suggest that reliance on expenditure data alone may lead to incomplete conclusions about drivers of environmental impacts.

Title: Trade integration, institutions, and environmental quality in Africa: Network-based approach

Title: Starting points of agroecological transitions in Africa: Why and how farm structure matter
Authors: Pierre Girard, Sara Mercandalli, David Berre, Nadine Andrieu, Rachel Bezner Kerr, Richard Coe, Benoît Dedieu, Sidney Madsen, Eric Scopel, Woinishet Asnake, Wolde Mekuria, Catherine Dembele, Aymen Frija, Yohana Haule, Christine Magaju, Dejene Kassahun Mengistu, Boko Michel Orounladji, Sitrakiniaina Raharimalala
Abstract: In sub-Saharan Africa, dominant agricultural models such as the Green Revolution have shown limitations, and agroecology is emerging as an alternative. Yet, empirical evidence remains scarce on who adopts agroecological practices and on what types of farms. A widely accepted narrative suggests that smallholders are more rooted in agroecological systems, while larger, better-endowed farms follow “conventional” models. This paper challenges that dualistic view by providing evidence of a wider set of relationship between farm structure and the diversity of agroecological practices across multiple African contexts. For this purpose it informs the diversity of existing patterns of farms structure and starting points of agroecological transition (AET) – defined as current state of agroecological principles implemented by farms along their trajectories. By situating these starting points within the socio-technical context of national and regional AET, we gain valuable insights into which farm structures support different agroecological principles, how socio-technical regime influence these dynamics, and what policy options emerge to foster AET. Using harmonized data from 2721 farms across nine study areas in six African countries, the article shows that starting points of agroecological transitions are highly diverse and influenced by farm structure. Three patterns emerge: smallest farms mostly combine autonomy and income diversification while larger farms tend to combine conventional intensification with crop-livestock integration. Other small to medium scale farms are characterized by more land allocated to legume contributing to soil health. Future agricultural policies should consider this diversity of patterns in providing locally-relevant support to promote sustainable transitions.

Title: The distributional impact of climate policy stringency in the European Union
Authors: Syeda Aimen Abbas, Thomas Kopp
Abstract: Environmental deterioration has become a central policy concern, reflected in initiatives such as the European Green Deal, which aim to steer European economies toward low-carbon development. While this transition is environmentally necessary, it may also generate uneven social and economic consequences. This study examines the distributional effects of environmental policy adoption and stringency in 26 European OECD countries over the period 1990–2022. Climate policy stringency is measured using the OECD's Climate Actions and Policies Measurement Framework (CAPMF), and income inequality is captured through three indicators: pre-tax national income Gini, disposable income Gini, and post-tax national income Gini. These measures allow assessment of inequality at different stages of the redistribution process. The analysis employs the Augmented Mean Group (AMG) estimator, which is suited to the panel's characteristics of slope heterogeneity, cross-sectional dependence, and potential endogeneity. The results show that greater climate policy stringency is associated with higher pre-tax and post-tax income inequality, suggesting that the costs of climate policy may fall disproportionately on lower-income groups. By contrast, the effect on disposable income inequality is not statistically significant, indicating that taxes and direct cash transfers can mitigate these adverse distributional effects. At the same time, the persistence of a positive association for post-tax inequality suggests that broader redistributive mechanisms, including in-kind transfers, do not fully offset them. These findings are robust across alternative specifications and estimators. Overall, the results suggest that a just green transition requires not only ambitious environmental policy, but also well-targeted redistributive measures to prevent inequality from widening.

Title: Assessing the chronic physical risks of climate change for the financial sector: A case study from Mexico's central Bank
Authors: Francisco Estrada, Miguel A. Altamirano del Carmen, Oscar Calderón-Bustamante, Rodrigo Muñoz-Sánchez, Alejandra Salazar, Luis O.L. Escobar-Farfán, W.J. Wouter Botzen, Serafín Martínez-Jaramillo, Stefano Battiston
Abstract: Mexico's Central Bank conducted a comprehensive climate risk assessment using a suite of global models to evaluate physical and transition risks. We focus on chronic physical risks, using a spatially explicit integrated assessment model that differentiates between urban and non-urban areas, capturing local climate impacts. Two complementary assessments are presented. First, we construct an index ranking the exposure of commercial bank loan portfolios based on local hazard, exposure and vulnerability measures. Second, we evaluate sectoral climate-related liability risk by attributing domestic/international economic damages from emissions using social-cost-of‑carbon estimates. Results reveal a strong concentration of chronic physical risk in central Mexico, highlighting the relevance of spatial granularity. We find substantial sectoral liability risks, particularly in the utilities and transportation sectors, driven largely by international damages. By incorporating multiple damage functions and probabilistic climate projections, we illustrate the uncertainty in impact estimates. Under a Current Policies scenario, economic losses could exceed 35% of Mexico's GDP by 2100 and surpass $20 trillion in present value, when accounting for the urban heat island effect. Paris-aligned scenarios substantially reduce these losses. This study emphasizes the usefulness of methods that exploit detailed, spatially explicit measures to improve estimation of exposure and liability risk of economic sectors.

Title: Resilience of pastoralist livelihoods in dry grazing systems under different preferences
Authors: Faan Langelaan, Frank van Langevelde, Florian Wagener
Abstract: The resilience literature has emphasized that in systems with alternative stable states, management must account not only for economic returns but also for the ability of desirable regimes to persist under disturbance. We contribute to this literature by analysing how pastoralists’ economic incentives affect the resilience of a bistable dryland grazing system. We incorporate pastoralist economic preferences into an existing dynamic eco-hydrological grazing model exhibiting bi-stability by coupling off-take decisions to a weighted utility function, describing value generated by animal sales and ongoing benefits like milk and wool. We find that higher livestock prices increase the system’s resilience to irreversible shocks if pastoralists maximize their utility. On the other hand, we find that higher prices do promote management strategies with less resilience to shocks that are reversible. This means that while damage to the ecosystem can be restored, economic livelihoods will come under stress doing so, because herd size and/or off-take levels have to be reduced during this process. In addition to these findings, we present a mapping of the trade-off between utility and resilience by plotting the efficient combinations on Pareto frontiers. Higher prices steepen these frontiers, making resilience increasingly costly in terms of forgone utility. This paper adds both to the literature about resilience in social-ecological systems in general and resilient management of rangelands prone to irreversible collapse specifically.

Title: Ecological and economic impacts of ocean deoxygenation on Pacific halibut fisheries: A multidisciplinary assessment of projected losses
Authors: Hongsik Kim, Louise Teh, Ilyass Dahmouni, Lubna Alam, Ibrahim Issifu, U. Rashid Sumaila
Abstract: The ocean has been losing oxygen content since at least the last century, and the rate of decline is accelerated by climate-induced changes like ocean warming, acidification, and anthropogenic driven nutrient load. Oxygen loss alters marine ecosystems and life, and consequently, human-wellbeing based on fisheries. Since marine fishes are known to be the most sensitive to deoxygenation, their mortality, growth, and abundance are affected by dissolved oxygen levels. Hence, fisheries relying on fish stocks are also impacted, with significant economic repercussions for society. The ability to estimate the economic impacts of deoxygenation on fisheries is hampered by the uncertain link between biogeochemical pathways and socio-economic impacts. Thus, we conducted a multidisciplinary modeling approach integrating ecological (metabolic rate index), biological (stock biomass dynamics), and economic (economic rent based on MSY) components to assess the economic ramifications of ocean deoxygenation (2020-2100) on the British Columbia Pacific halibut fishery.We find that under conditions of up to 40% reduction in dissolved oxygen and a 30% increase in temperature by 2100, Pacific halibut biomass could decrease by 66% ~ 89%. This significant decrease in catch could lead to an estimated cumulative economic loss of around $100 million by 2100. Ripple effects throughout the supply chain, including secondary (processing) and tertiary industries (distribution, marketing), could cause an additional economic impact loss of up to $197 million by 2100. Therefore, our study suggests it is crucial for the Pacific Halibut Commission and fisheries to incorporate adaptation and mitigation strategies to counteract ongoing deoxygenation and warming.

Title: Modelling degrowth policies with system dynamics: Towards policy coherence
Authors: Karel Zwetsloot, David Collste, Therese Bennich, Thomas Hahn, Matteo Pedercini
Abstract: • We simulate degrowth policy interactions in a high-income country. • Degrowth policies can reduce environmental pressures and advance social equity. • Isolated policies create trade-offs; coherent policy packages can resolve them. • Producing less while redistributing more improves social-ecological outcomes. • Short-term fiscal feasibility contrasts with long-term public debt challenges.

Title: Shades of outrage? Socio-economic causes of environmental degradation and stated WTP
Authors: Jorge H. Garcia, Fernando Carriazo, Fredrik Carlsson
Abstract: This study explicitly acknowledges that environmental damage typically occurs within a social context. We conducted a willingness-to-pay (WTP) survey of 844 individuals to measure the welfare losses induced by an environmental externality: we used two treatments in which the socioeconomic background of those who caused the externality varied. The treatments varied in the degree of control (or agency) that the generators of the externality had over their actions. The study finds no statistical difference in mean WTP across treatments, indicating no evidence of Kahneman's “outrage effect,” whereby individuals are particularly upset by what they regard as intentional harms.

Title: Open veins: Drain from Latin America through ecologically unequal exchange
Authors: Morena Hanbury Lemos, Jason Hickel
Abstract: In Open Veins of Latin America (1971), Eduardo Galeano argued that colonial interventions in Latin America organised the regional economy around raw material exports and drained the continent of valuable resources and labour, producing conditions of underdevelopment. Scholars have argued that this dynamic continues today, where the suppression of prices and input costs in peripheral regions enables the global North to appropriate resources and value through ‘unequal exchange’. Building on this analysis and grounded in the Marxist tradition of dependency theory, this study empirically assesses Latin America's position with respect to unequal exchange of natural resources and labour embodied in trade. We use environmentally extended multi-regional input-output (EEMRIO) analysis to measure net flows of embodied materials (biomass, fossil fuels, minerals, and metals), land, and labour between Latin America, the global North, China, and the rest of the global South (1995 to 2020) across seven sectors, along with wage compensation against the labour flows. We find that Latin America has suffered a large drain of all resources to the North over the period. In 2020, the North net-appropriated 935 million tons of materials (including biomass, minerals, metals, and fossil fuels), 4 million km 2 of land, and 53 billion hours of labour (worth €816 billion in Northern wages) from Latin America, mostly consumed as manufactured goods and services. We find that Latin America's position in the world economy is increasingly ‘peripheral’ in character. It remains a major supplier of primary commodities to the North, experiences a greater per capita drain of biomass, metals, and land than China or the rest of the global South, and disproportionately suffers the ecological damages of Northern consumption.

Title: Analyzing citizens' preferences for sufficiency policy in municipalities — An experimental approach
Authors: Tonja Iten, Max Rudolf, Manuel Suter, Maritza Satama, Marco Pütz, Roland Olschewski
Abstract: Sufficiency policies address unsustainable consumption and production patterns by promoting ways of living and economies that prioritize “enough” over “more,” reducing resource use while safeguarding fundamental human needs. Public support is crucial for the effective implementation of sufficiency policies, yet empirical research on citizens' preferences and their underlying mechanisms remains scarce—particularly concerning quantitative studies and with respect to the municipal level. Thus, this study investigates public support for sufficiency policies in municipalities, focusing on governable factors that shape citizens' preferences. Taking Switzerland as a case study, a nationwide representative online survey ( N = 1052) was conducted that combined a discrete choice and a framing experiment. Our results suggest that citizens' preferences for implementing sufficiency policies depend on the targeted policy sector, measure type, and procedural fairness. First, respondents indicated low support for housing sufficiency measures, opting instead for food or mobility sufficiency measures. Second, preferences related to measure type depend on the designation and selection of specific policy measures, which makes general conclusions about type alone difficult. Third, respondents placed considerable emphasis on procedural fairness, favoring passive involvement (being kept informed) in the implementation process. In terms of strategically employing co-benefit framing to increase policy support, evidence on framing effects is mixed but indicates that social co-benefits must be chosen carefully. Overall, we conclude that there is a modest but consistent majority in favor of implementing sufficiency policies at the municipal level. • Sufficiency policy aims to reduce resource use while fundamental human needs are met. • The study analyses preferences for sufficiency policies at the municipal level. • Public support exists, even when behavioral or financial costs are made explicit. • Citizens prefer sufficiency measures related to food or mobility over housing. • Whether social co-benefits raise policy support depends on their specific nature.

Title: Towards a typology of residential energy consumers: Social context and awareness as predictors of energy-efficient household behaviors in the United States
Authors: Erin Heinz, Benjamin K. Sovacool, Thomas Kwan, Johan Nordensvärd, Frauke Urban, Muhammad Asif, Weimin Zhang, Patrik Thollander, Patrik Rohdin, Niklas Arvidsson
Abstract: Residential or household energy use in heating, cooling, and lighting must become more efficient to advance residential decarbonization and meet 2050 global climate targets. This study presents a typology of social impacts and behaviors, emphasizing normative community roles in decarbonization of residential buildings. We examine efficiency-related behaviors in the private sphere including lighting, air-conditioning use, and building upgrades using a nationally representative United States dataset ( n = 1002). We analyze social encouragement from friends, family, and workplace. OLS analyses show that these social normative pressures significantly predict ongoing energy-efficiency behaviors, including both developing behaviors (i.e. managing air conditioning, β = 0.220, p < .001) and habitual behaviors (i.e. turning off lights, β = 0.163, p < .001). Logit models further indicate that social influence significantly increases the likelihood of one-off efficiency upgrades in the home (b = 0.336, p < .001). Results additionally distinguish three behavioral profiles characterized by differing levels of awareness of emissions and energy issues and varying degrees of peer influence. Across profiles, contextual factors such as awareness and social encouragement outweigh demographic predictors and independently shape efficiency behaviors. These findings substantiate the importance of social context in household energy management. We conclude with policy recommendations.

Title: Designing MEMME – A conceptual material and energy metabolism model for economies
Authors: Laura Felício, Fridolin Krausmann, Tânia Sousa
Abstract: Abstract Energy and materials drive the socioeconomic processes of the economy, acquiring economic value through physical and chemical transformations. Consequently, understanding an economy requires analyzing not only its monetary flows but also its biophysical flows and stocks. However, integrating material and energy perspectives into a unified analytical framework remains a challenge that existing approaches have only partially addressed. This study introduces the Material and Energy Metabolism Model for Economies (MEMME), a new conceptual biophysical model that provides a consistent and balanced accounting in both mass and energy units. MEMME focuses on material, energy, and food and feed transformations, integrating stocks and flows, to enable a more comprehensive analysis of social metabolism. It presents new indicators that improve our understanding of resource use, transformation efficiency, and their connection to economic activity, including a biophysical economic productivity indicator (BioEP), which measures how effectively physical outputs (materials and useful exergy) contribute to generating economic output. The Portuguese case study (1970–2022) shows that resource use increased and stock grew, while efficiency gains were modest and did not reduce overall consumption. BioEP reveals that Portugal became more efficient at converting resources into useful flows, but less efficient at translating those flows into economic value, highlighting a tradeoff between efficiency and productivity. BioEP, however, also indicates absolute decoupling between 2000 and 2008. MEMME provides a consistent framework to derive such integrated insights.

Title: Rethinking the use of the residual value method for ecosystem services valuation
Authors: Sean Pascoe, Koenraad Van Landeghem, Gabriela Scheufele, Solomon Abrahams
Abstract: A critical component of ecosystem accounts is the monetary value of ecosystem services. This requires the estimation of an exchange value for the ecosystem services, which represents the value the ecosystem service would receive if a market for the service existed. The UN System of Environmental-Economic Accounting – Ecosystem Accounting (SEEA EA) endorses a range of different approaches for deriving estimates of the exchange value of the ecosystem services. One such approach that has been widely adopted is to derive an estimate of resource rent based on the “residual value method”. This assumes that resource rent – a measure of the value of the ecosystem input into production – is equivalent to the residual value after all costs (including normal returns to manufactured capital) have been deducted from revenue. Several issues exist with this approach, foremost being that it does not explicitly consider the ecosystem service to be an input into the production process, and in some applications, has resulted in negative estimates of the value of the ecosystem service. In this paper, we highlight the issues around the use of the residual value method, and propose that it is not an appropriate method for use in estimating exchange prices for ecosystem services for use in ecosystem accounts. Instead, we suggest that exchange values for ecosystem services be based on one of the other SEEA EA endorsed approaches.

Title: Beyond carbon sequestration: Swedish farmers' preferences and trade-offs between co-benefits of climate change mitigation measures
Authors: Harold Opdenbosch, Emilia Mattsson, Oyakhilomen Oyinbo, Jens Rommel, Helena Hansson, Gordana Manevska-Tasevska
Abstract: The mitigation of greenhouse gas emissions is a central policy concern in agriculture, reflected through voluntary contractual measures in the Common Agricultural Policy. The literature suggests that farmers' motivation for participating in mitigation measures does not necessarily originate in climate consciousness nor a sense of responsibility for mitigation, but rather in the co-benefits that they can bring. This paper investigates farmers' preferences for climate-related and non-climate co-benefits of mitigation measures, specifically carbon sequestration, biodiversity and soil health, using the cover cropping eco-scheme as a case study. We elicit trade-offs between monetary and non-monetary utility values associated with the co-benefits, alongside farmers' attitudes and identities, using a survey among Swedish farmers ( n = 179). Results reveal two distinct classes: class 1 reflects “responsive farmers” due to their greater sensitivity to the non-monetary attributes in the utility function and their positive and significant attitudes towards cover cropping, while class 2 refers to “conventional farmers”, with a stronger preference for the status quo and monetary utility values. Responsive farmers are prepared to incur costs, such as accepting reductions in subsidy payments, to support agri-environmental and climate outcomes. Soil health emerges as the most preferred co-benefit, likely due to its more immediate and tangible private returns, including improved yields, compared with the broader public goods associated with biodiversity and carbon sequestration. Farmers' underlying attitudes towards the cover cropping eco-scheme, alongside farmers' age, are the main source of unobserved heterogeneity in preferences and trade-offs.

Title: Revealing the abatement costs of soil erosion: a cost frontier approach
Authors: Andreas Eder
Abstract: • We propose a cost frontier approach for estimating pollution abatement cost (PAC). • We integrate the materials balance in soil erosion and PAC estimation. • We reveal farms’ costs of participating in a soil conservation program. • Farms located in areas with higher erosion risk tend to have lower abatement costs. • Targeting criteria for allocation of funds could have improved cost-effectiveness.

Title: Virtual water in global supply chains: Trade structure, industrial composition, and policy levers
Authors: Weimin Jiang, Jiajing Sun, Michael Cole, Yuanbo Zhang

Title: Limits of low-cost environmentalism: Experimental evidence on tap- versus bottled-water consumption
Authors: Sarah Gomm, Jale Tosun, Thomas Bernauer
Abstract: Many studies show that individuals are more likely to engage in voluntary pro-environmental behavior when the personal costs of doing so are low. Policymakers, in turn, are interested in identifying such opportunities in order to minimize heavy-handed government interventions and thus maintain public support for environmental policy. We revisit this issue by examining a case where low-cost environmentalism should be prevalent: choosing tap water over bottled water, a form of pro-environmental behavior that not only saves consumers’ money but also has a very substantial environmental protection benefit. Using an experimental approach with a large representative sample of Switzerland’s adult resident population (N=6893), we tested whether increasing awareness of three key advantages of tap water — (1) health effects, (2) environmental benefits, and (3) cost savings — could shift consumption behavior toward tap water. We find that only combined information addressing all three aspects increases the likelihood of choosing tap water over bottled water, and even this effect is very small. These results suggest that even under seemingly ideal conditions for voluntary pro-environmental action, information campaigns alone may be insufficient for reducing the environmental footprint of consumption, and that policymakers should consider measures providing stronger (dis-)incentives in this domain.

Title: Moral persuasion and normative regulation: How transgenerational education influences green consumption behavior with varying power distance orientation
Authors: Feiyu Chen, Tong Zhang, Honghui Cai, Zhexin Zhu

Title: Biodiversity impact of agricultural products in France: Greater differences across product types than food quality schemes
Authors: Sarah Huet, Abdoul Diallo, Julie Regolo, Ainhoa Ihasusta, Ludovic Arnaud, Valentin Bellassen
Abstract: Although agriculture contributes to four main drivers of biodiversity loss, the impact assessment of food products remains limited to either in situ measurements that preclude generalization or to systematic models that are not calibrated on in situ data. Here we describe the BVIAS (Biodiversity Value Increment from Agricultural Statistics) model, which estimates the biodiversity impact of food products using accountancy data and public statistics for use in environmental labeling schemes or other purposes. Going beyond existing methods, BVIAS accounts for the main drivers of biodiversity loss related to agriculture, relies on a large farm dataset (>5000 farms), and is calibrated using in situ data from the literature. We apply it to compare major Food Quality Schemes (FQSs) to their conventional counterparts. We show that only explicit requirements (e.g., ban on pesticides, grass-fed content) in FQS specifications lead to significant differences in practice. Consistent with the literature, we find that organic farms have a lower biodiversity impact on a per-hectare basis, as well as those producing Comté (Protected Designation of Origin), but lower yields offset this local benefit, resulting in a higher impact per ton. However, the biodiversity impact gap between product types (here milk vs. cereals) is far greater than the difference between FQS and conventional versions of the same product. This study highlights that, for environmental labeling, the distinction between product types is more important than the distinction between FQS and conventional.

Title: The heat is on: Implications of extreme temperatures on productive and defensive inputs in West Africa
Authors: Martin Paul Jr. Tabe-Ojong, Jourdain C. Lokossou
